item.title: PM confirms the next general elections will be held under the current electoral system and by Feb 6th 2027
item.description: With some creating confusion by saying that the general elections will not be held during the required legal timeline under the 2013 Constitution, and uncertainties surrounding drastic changes to the electoral system that could affect the Fijian Elections Office's preparations with only about 8 weeks to go for the Writ of Elections to be issued, Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka has today made it cl
item.content:encoded:
With some creating confusion by saying that the general elections will not be held during the required legal timeline under the 2013 Constitution, and uncertainties surrounding drastic changes to the electoral system that could affect the Fijian Elections Office's preparations with only about 8 weeks to go for the Writ of Elections to be issued, Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka has today made it clear that logically, the next general elections will be held under the current electoral system.

Rabuka made this clear in an exclusive interview when fijivillage News asked him on whether he can confirm to the people if the next general elections which has to be held by February 6th 2027, will be held under the current electoral system.

We also asked Rabuka whether any electoral changes, including those in the Constitution Amendment Bill on the drawing up of electoral boundaries if a multi constituency electoral system is approved, will be used in the elections after the 2027 elections as we need the boundaries drawn up, and population figures based on the census, which is scheduled to be held next year.

In his response, the Prime Minister says the constituency boundaries have to be drawn up and the census will take place next year.

Rabuka says the census data will provide the essential information for the Electoral Commission to do their work in time for any elections eventually the next government will face.

In a recent interview, Supervisor of Elections, Ana Mataiciwa had said that the Fijian Elections Office is ready to deliver the general elections under the current system based on the legal timeline where the last day for the Writ of Elections to be issued by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister is December 24th this year and the last date for the general elections is February 6th 2027.

She had said it would be impossible to deliver the general elections operationally within this timeframe if drastic changes are made to the electoral system including a multi constituency system.

The transitional provision of the Constitution Amendment Bill states that on the commencement of the law, the current parliament continues until it is dissolved or ends its term in accordance with section 58 of the 2013 Constitution.

This means the next general elections will be held under the legal timetable specified in the 2013 Constitution - the last day for the Writ of Elections to be issued is 24th December this year and the last day for the general elections is February 6th next year.

It is also stated that the 2026 Constitution Amendment Bill, if passed, will come into force on 31st March 2028.

However the President may, by Proclamation published in the Gazette, fix a date earlier than 31st March 2028.

Despite the commencement, section 58 of the 2013 Constitution continues to apply to the current parliament, and the maximum term of the current parliament remains 4 years from the date of the first meeting of the first Parliament.

The Constitution Amendment Bill also proposes the retention of a 55 member Parliament however a system is proposed where 33 constituency members or such number as Parliament may by written law

prescribe, which includes 5 maritime constituencies chosen directly by the registered voters of those constituencies in a first-past-the-post election; and 22 party list members or such number as Parliament may by written law prescribe, allocated to political parties in proportion to the total number of votes for the candidates of that party in the constituency seats.

Parliament or the House of Representatives is to be composed in a manner that reflects, as closely as practicable, the proportion of votes cast for political parties.

A political party is entitled to proportional representation if it secures not less than

Constituency seats won are deducted from each party’s proportional entitlement, with the balance filled from party lists.

The Party list seats must be allocated in accordance with a written law prescribing an appropriate mathematical rounding method, which rounds fractions to whole numbers to determine seat allocations.

Candidates unaffiliated with a political party may contest constituency seats, and if elected, serve as independent members without affecting proportional allocation.

A candidate of a party can stand for election in a constituency seat and be included in the party’s list for a party list seat.

The Bill says Parliament may provide, by written law, for temporary special measures relating to the way in which party lists must be constituted, for example measures to ensure, as far as possible, equal numbers of male and female candidates; or measures to otherwise facilitate diverse representation on party lists.

The maritime constituencies are Rotuma, Yasawa, Kadavu, Lomaiviti and Lau.

A candidate for election to the House of Representatives must be either nominated by a registered political party or nominated as an independent candidate in accordance with the laws governing elections.

A person may be a candidate for election to the House of Representatives only if the person is a citizen of Fiji; is qualified to be registered as a voter and is registered on the Register o f

Voters; is ordinarily resident in Fiji for at least 2 years immediately before being nominated; is not an undischarged bankrupt; is not a member of the Electoral Commission and has not been a member of that Commission at any time during the 4 years immediately before being nominated; is not subject to a sentence of imprisonment when nominated; has not, at any time during the 8 years immediately before being nominated, been convicted of an offence under any law for which the maximum penalty is a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more; and has not, in the 5 years immediately before being nominated, been found guilty of any offence under a law relating to elections, registration of political parties or registration of voters.

The total number of candidates that a political party may nominate for any general election must not be more than the total number of seats in the House of Representatives, and the total number of candidates that a political party may nominate for any by-election must not be more than the total number of vacant seats in the House of Representatives for which the by-election is held.

If a seat in the House of Representatives becomes vacant, the vacancy must be filled in the case of a constituency seat, by a by-election; and in the case of a party list seat, by the next candidate on the party list; or if there is no next candidate on the party list, by a by-election.

The Bill also proposes the House of Representatives continues for 5 years from the date of its first meeting after a general election of the members of the House of Representatives, unless sooner dissolved in accordance with the Constitution.

item.content:encoded:
Supervisor of Elections, Ana Mataiciwa will appear on fijivillage Straight Talk With Vijay Narayan at 7pm tomorrow.

The show will focus on the state of preparedness of the Fijian Elections Office for the proposed national referendum on December 9th and the next general elections which has to be held by February 6th 2027, the nationwide voter registration underway, changes to the electoral laws and the impact on the voters and the country, and the impact of any drastic changes with two months to go for the last day for the Writ of Elections to be issued on December 24th 2026 amongst other issues.

Parent raises concerns over children's safety with broken bottles and other paraphernalia litter Komo Park in Samabula
item.description: A concerned parent is raising concerns on the safety of children playing at Komo Park in Samabula which is littered with broken bottles and other paraphernalia. Jason Singh says he has chased children away several times from the area where the broken bottles are lying around but they would usually return when he leaves.
item.content:encoded:
A concerned parent is raising concerns on the safety of children playing at Komo Park in Samabula which is littered with broken bottles and other paraphernalia.

Jason Singh says he has chased children away several times from the area where the broken bottles are lying around but they would usually return when he leaves.

He says his child who is a student at the nearby Samabula Primary School would usually play with his friends and other students at the park.

Singh is highlighting that there are broken bottles all over the place as well as smoking apparatus for marijuana that litter the ground.

He says that he has highlighted this issue several times with the Suva City Council but they have not taken any action in regards to his complaints.

We have sought comments from the SCC and Police.

item.title: Ba businessman lodges cyberbullying complaint against Bainivalu, Minister denies intent to ridicule
item.description: Ba business owner Sevanaia Levuidali says he has lodged a complaint against Minister for Fisheries Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of cyberbullying after she posted a video of him falling off a chair while making a submission to the Joint Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 202 in Ba. Police have also confirmed to fijivillage News that Levuidali filed a report at the Ba Police Station th
item.content:encoded:
Ba business owner Sevanaia Levuidali says he has lodged a complaint against Minister for Fisheries Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of cyberbullying after she posted a video of him falling off a chair while making a submission to the Joint Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 202 in Ba.

Police have also confirmed to fijivillage News that Levuidali filed a report at the Ba Police Station this morning against the Minister for cyber-bullying.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Levuidali questioned why Bainivalu had shared the video on facebook, which was taken from a Fiji Government livestream of the public consultation at the Ba Market Bure.

Levuidali says he does not understand why Bainivalu chose to post the part of the video showing him falling off the chair.

He has raised concerns about cyberbullying and referred to previous incidents involving members of the Government.

He mentioned former Minister for Women and Children and current Information Minister Lynda Tabuya and former Attorney General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga, in his comments about cyberbullying within political circles.

Levuidali says he believes the incident raises questions about the use of social media by public figures.

In response, Minister Bainivalu says she did not intend to ridicule Levuidali after posting a video of him falling off a chair on her official facebook page.

She says the video also shows the part of his submission in which he was ridiculing the panel.

Bainivalu says the consultations are public hearings that allow the public to engage in different forms of discussion, adding that it was unfortunate Levuidali fell off his chair.

She says the videos are intended to show the public that the consultations are open to everyone, regardless of whether they sit, stand or speak while facing away from the panel.

Bainivalu also says people should prepare themselves well before attending the consultations.

item.title: Rakiraki farmer calls for up to one year of public consultations on Constitution Bill
item.description: While making his submission to the Joint Parliamentary Special Committee at Rakiraki Hall, Ali says every Fijian should be given enough time to understand the proposed constitutional changes and contribute to the process. He believes rushing the consultations could repeat mistakes of the past and affect public confidence in the constitutional review process.
item.content:encoded:
While making his submission to the Joint Parliamentary Special Committee at Rakiraki Hall, Ali says every Fijian should be given enough time to understand the proposed constitutional changes and contribute to the process.

He believes rushing the consultations could repeat mistakes of the past and affect public confidence in the constitutional review process.

Ali, who is a sugarcane and cassava farmer, also raised concerns about a change in the scheduled time for the consultation in Rakiraki.

He says residents were initially informed that the consultation would begin at 6pm, but the time was later changed to 10am.

Ali believes this may have contributed to the low turnout, as some residents may have relied on the original schedule.

He says some communities in Rakiraki have limited or no mobile network coverage, making it difficult for residents to receive updates shared only on Facebook.

Ali says important government announcements should also be communicated through the Provincial Administrator's Office and advisory councillors to ensure information reaches people in rural communities.

He stresses that the Constitution is the supreme law of the country and that all Fijians should have a fair opportunity to contribute to any proposed changes.

Ali also believes the findings of the Constitution Review Commission should be respected and reflected in the proposed amendments.

On other issues raised in his submission, Ali is calling for Fiji to remain a secular State and has proposed replacing references to Christianity in the proposed amendments, with references to religion and family values to protect the rights of people from different religious backgrounds.

He has also raised concerns about the proposed provision relating to the chastisement of children, saying parents should take greater responsibility for teaching their children discipline and respect.

Ali is also calling for stronger constitutional protection of freehold land, saying landowners need assurance that their property rights will remain protected in the future.

He says freehold land ownership is particularly important for minority communities.

Ali has urged the Committee to carefully consider public submissions and ensure that the final constitutional amendments reflect the views of all Fijians.

Meanwhile, consultation will be held at Rakiraki Village Hall in Navutulevu from 4pm to 6pm today.

Tomorrow, consultations will be held at Wailotua Village Hall in Wainibuka from 10am to midday and at Korovou Primary School Hall from 3pm to 5pm.
